title: consumption-experience-guidelines-for-saas-integrations-2026-07-01
author: Priya Shah
content:
Overview

This page defines the recommended consumption experience and operational playbook for SaaS vendors integrating Redwood Inference into customer-facing product features. It consolidates product, pricing, technical, and telemetry guidelines so that integrations are predictable for customers and sustainable for Redwood.

Goals

- Provide a prescriptive, low-friction onboarding flow for SaaS teams (self-serve + light sales assistance).
- Ensure observable cost and performance characteristics per-route for multi-tenant SaaS products.
- Offer clear packaging choices and migration paths from free/dev tiers to committed capacity.
- Reduce customer support volume related to consumption surprises and billing disputes.

Non-goals

- This doc is not a full SDK reference (see SDK guides).
- It does not replace vertical compliance playbooks for regulated industries (see security-and-compliance).

Audience

- Product managers at SaaS vendors evaluating Redwood for feature-level inference.
- Engineering leads implementing server-side integrations and observability.
- Solutions engineers and account teams supporting trial-to-paid conversions.

High-level consumption patterns covered

1) Real-time user-facing generation (sub-300ms target for short prompts).
2) Background batch inference (embeddings, reranking, summarization).
3) Hybrid: user-triggered async pipelines with cached quick replies.

Key design principles

- Route at the "feature" level, not the customer level: each product feature should map to a Redwood route with distinct SLOs and cost budgets.
- Expose per-route token and latency telemetry to customers where practical (dashboard and CSV exports).
- Default to conservative batching and prefix caching; provide opt-ins for aggressive batching for price-sensitive workloads.
- Offer predictable fallbacks: define variant fallback chains (same fidelity -> lower cost variant -> expedited lightweight response).

Packaging and pricing guidance (recommendations for go-to-market)

- Standard integration packaging: three pre-built SKUs for SaaS feature consumption: Starter (trial/dev), Business (pay-as-you-go), and Committed (discounted reserved capacity).
- Suggested SKU attributes and guide:

| SKU | Typical tenant profile | Billing model | Recommended per-feature guardrails |
|-----|------------------------|---------------|-------------------------------------|
| Starter | Early users, POC | Free credits then pay-as-you-go | Soft quota 5k tokens/month, default low-burst rate |
| Business | Growing customers | Usage-based monthly invoice | Per-route budget cap, optional alerting |
| Committed | High-volume tenants | Monthly committed commit + overage | Dedicated route weighting, SLA, custom fallback |

- Price guidance examples (illustrative; teams should set final pricing in conjunction with GtM):
  - Short text gen ( < 512 tokens): base 0.6 USD per 1k input+output tokens for pay-as-you-go; committed discounts 30–45%.
  - Embeddings: 0.25 USD per 1k embedding units; committed discounts 25–40%.
  - Background batch jobs: negotiate bulk price or use per-job crediting with tiered rates.

Operational controls to implement in SaaS product

- Per-feature rate limits and token budgets: keep default conservative (e.g., 100 requests/min feature-global) and allow admin elevation.
- Traffic shaping: prefer token-budget enforcement over hard request-rejects; return cached placeholder responses with an explanatory header when budget exhausted.
- Fallback policy: define an ordered list (primary high-fidelity model -> optimized quantized variant -> semantic cache retrieval) with clear latency/quality expectations.

Telemetry and SLOs (what Redwood exposes and what SaaS should monitor)

Redwood-provided telemetry (available in Console and via API):
- Per-route: tokens consumed (input/output), request count, P50/P95/P99 latency, error rate by class, model variant used, fallback events.
- Per-tenant (when using tenant-routing): aggregate token burn and budget utilization.
- Billing: daily invoice estimates and forecasted 30-day burn.

Recommended SaaS SLOs to publish internally:
- Feature availability: 99.9% goal for hosted features on Business SKUs; 99.95% for Committed.
- Latency targets: P95 < 300ms for short-turnaround features; P95 < 1500ms allowed for complex generation with streaming.
- Cost variance guard: monitor rolling 7-day cost variance vs. forecast; trigger review above 20% variance.

Telemetry implementation checklist

1. Wire per-route Redwood metrics into the product's observability pipeline (Datadog/Prometheus) via Console exports or the telemetry API.
2. Create dashboards: cost-by-feature, latency-by-feature, fallback-rate-by-feature.
3. Set alerting:
   - Alert1: fallback-rate > 3% sustained for 30m -> notify infra/product.
   - Alert2: daily forecasted burn > committed capacity by 10% -> escalate to account management.

SDK and API considerations for SaaS integrations

- Use named routes: each feature must call Redwood with a stable route identifier to separate telemetry, budgets, and rollouts.
- Idempotency keys: recommend per-user request idempotency for retry-safe UX for short-turnaround endpoints.
- Embedding retention: commit to retention tiers for embeddings consistent with privacy agreements (see data-residency-and-retention).

Example request snippet (recommended pattern):

curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" -H "X-Redwood-Route: product-search-autocomplete" -d '{"input":"Summarize recent activity for user X","max_tokens":120,"user_id":"tenant-123|user-456"}'

Migration playbook: trial -> paid -> committed capacity

1. Trial phase (self-serve): enable the Starter SKU with an onboarding guide and prefilled route templates. Provide an Export of 30-day forecast for customers near commit thresholds.
2. Conversion to Business (pay-as-you-go):
   - Step A: Send usage digest and recommended per-feature budgets.
   - Step B: Add per-feature quota APIs into admin console.
   - Step C: Enable per-feature alerting for customers.
3. Commit negotiation and Dedicated/Committed migration:
   - Step A: Run a 14-day usage stabilization period with elevated telemetry retention (30d).
   - Step B: Execute capacity reservation plan with infra and enable SLAs.
   - Step C: Provide a backwards-compatible testing window to validate performance under dedicated capacity.

Rollout and compatibility guidance

- Canary deploys: start with 5% of production traffic for 48h, monitor latency, fallback rate, and quality regressions (see quality-guardrails).
- Compatibility matrix: document model variants and quantization profiles that are approved for each SKU and list expected latency/cost per 1k tokens for the typical hardware profile.

Quality and customer communications

- Quality guardrails: maintain a small prompt set per feature used for daily regression checks. If the new variant increases fallback rate or decreases relevance > 5% on the prompt set, block rollout.
- Customer-facing messaging: produce templates for escalation emails explaining billing spikes, fallback behavior, and upgrade recommendations.

Support playbook (operational steps for customer success)

1. Initial triage: confirm route identifier, route-level budgets, and recent fallback events.
2. Simulated repro: run the customer's failing prompt set against the same model variant as their traffic (use the sandbox runner).
3. Rapid mitigation: temporarily increase per-route budget or switch route to a lower-cost variant if a billing spike is the cause.
4. Root cause: evaluate whether the cause is product-side (infinite-loop prompt, bot traffic), model-side (regression), or configuration (missing caching).
